findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the shell command
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell metacharacters—for example, the valid Git ref `topic;id`—`exec()` interprets them and executes additional commands with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` passed the branch as one opaque argument.

findings.title: [P2] Return the Git child process directly
findings.body: Callers now receive the shell process created by `exec()` rather than the Git process returned by `execFile()`. Killing that process does not reliably terminate its Git child, allowing work or output to continue after callers consider the operation cancelled.

findings.title: [P2] Keep the returned child tied to the Git process
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than `git`. On Windows, or any shell that does not replace itself with Git, calling `.kill()` on a long-running `showBranch()` terminates only the shell and can leave Git running. This breaks cancellation and may emit the shell’s `exit` before Git has stopped, consuming resources and producing output after callers consider the operation cancelled.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch name out of the shell command
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell, so a branch such as `topic;id` or `topic$(command)` executes arbitrary commands. These are valid Git branch names, so even legitimate input can trigger shell interpretation. The previous `execFile()` call passed the branch as an opaque argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore argument-separated execution to prevent shell injection
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell and interpolates `branch` verbatim. Any attacker-controlled value such as `main; arbitrary-command` executes that command with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile()` implementation treated the branch as a single Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
